text:
Help me write an announcement to our staff. I'm the COO of a credit union with 7 branches. We're closing the Maple Street and Route 9 branches on March 31 and moving the people who work there to a new member phone and chat center.

Facts:
- The two branches have 14 staff between them. Every one of them is offered a job in the phone and chat center at the same pay or higher.
- Visits to those two branches fell 44% over the last three years. Phone and chat contacts across the credit union went up 60%.
- Members calling us now wait an average of 9 minutes on hold.
- The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. The branches were open 9 to 5. Shifts will rotate.
- Staff in the center can work from home two days a week after 90 days of training.
- Anyone who doesn't take the new role gets 2 weeks of pay for every year they've worked here.

I want the announcement to say that this change will make everyone's job better. About 400 words, sent by email from me.

Before I draft, there's one problem with the main message and a few gaps to fill.

**"This change will make everyone's job better" goes further than your facts do.** Some of the facts back it up: same pay or higher, a job for all 14 people, working from home two days a week after training, and the chance to fix a 9-minute hold time that members are probably taking out on staff. But the move also takes people from a 9-to-5 day to rotating shifts that can run until 8 p.m. For anyone with childcare, a second job or a long commute, that's a worse job. Some of the 14 will decide not to take it. They'll read "better for everyone" as spin and trust the rest of the email less.

A version your facts do support: **"This change protects every job, fixes a real problem for our members, and gives people options they don't have at a branch, like working from home. It also asks something real of the people moving: new hours and new work. Here's what we're doing to make that fair."** Name the hard part once and plainly, then answer it. I'd recommend this version, but it's your call. If you still want the bold version, I'll write it.

**Questions. Short answers are fine, and "don't know" is fine:**

1. **How do the rotating shifts work?** How many late shifts in a typical week or month, is there extra pay for evenings, and can people say what shifts they prefer? This will be staff's biggest worry, and these details are the only real answer to it.
2. **Will the 14 hear this in person before the email goes out?** And does the email go to all staff or only to them? Learning about your own job change from a mass email causes the most damage, so the email should be able to say they've already been told, or will be today.
3. **What is the deadline to accept or decline the new role?** Is there a cap on the severance, and does it come with anything else, like health coverage or a reference?
4. **Where is the center, and when does training start?** Is the 90 days of training paid at full rate? Do people keep their seniority and unused time off?
5. **What can you say to the other five branches?** When two branches close, everyone else wonders if theirs is next. If you can say something true, like "no other closures are planned," it belongs in the email. If you can't, I'll leave it out and won't hint at it.
6. **Is there anything staff will find out anyway?** For example, how members at those two branches will be served after March 31, or any earlier closures or promises they'll remember. It's better to address that in the email than have them hear it elsewhere.

Once you reply, I'll write the roughly 400-word email for you to sign.

Your version is fine. Better to say what's true than "better for everyone."

1. I don't know how many late shifts or whether there's evening pay. Staff with the most years here pick shifts first. I can't promise anyone 9 to 5.
2. I don't know yet.
3. Written offers go out by February 14, and decisions are due March 1. I don't know about a cap, health coverage or references. Anyone who takes the new role and wants out within 6 months can still get the severance. Anyone who wants a one-on-one with HR can have one.
4. The center is at our main office on Elm Avenue. I don't know when training starts, whether it's paid at full rate, or what happens with seniority and time off.
5. I don't know.
6. Our current phone team lost about 30% of its people last year, and staff know that. I also can't keep the two branches open, so that decision is final. I don't know how members at those branches will be served after March 31.

I wrote the email around the claim you approved: every job is protected and the reason is real, but the new role asks something real of the people moving. It's about 430 words.

<final_document>
Subject: Maple Street and Route 9 branches will close March 31

To all staff,

I'm writing to tell you about a decision that affects all of us, and 14 of our colleagues most of all. On March 31, we will close our Maple Street and Route 9 branches. Everyone who works at those two branches will be offered a job in our new member phone and chat center at the main office on Elm Avenue, at the same pay or higher. Every one of them has a job here if they want it.

Here's why. Over the last three years, visits to those two branches fell 44%. Over the same period, phone and chat contacts across the credit union went up 60%. Members who call us now wait an average of 9 minutes on hold. Our members have changed how they reach us, and we haven't kept up. This decision is final.

The new role is a real change, and I won't pretend otherwise. The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays, and shifts will rotate. Staff with the most years here will choose shifts first, but I can't promise anyone a 9-to-5 schedule. After 90 days of training, center staff can work from home two days a week.

Many of you know our current phone team lost about 30% of its people last year. That's a fair thing to worry about. Part of what has made that work hard is too many calls for too few people, and adding 14 colleagues who know our members is part of how we fix it. We've also built in a safety net: if you take the new role and decide within six months that it isn't right for you, you can still leave with the full severance.

What happens next:

- Written offers go out by February 14.
- Decisions are due by March 1.
- If you choose not to take the new role, you'll receive two weeks of pay for every year you've worked here.
- Anyone who wants a one-on-one with HR to talk through their situation can have one.

Some questions don't have answers yet, including when training starts and how members at Maple Street and Route 9 will be served after March 31. I'll share those answers as soon as we have them, and I won't guess before then.

To the staff at Maple Street and Route 9: you know our members, and that is exactly what members on the other end of the phone need. Whatever you decide, thank you for the work you've done.

Chief Operating Officer
</final_document>

Before you send it:

- **The 14 should hear this before anyone else.** If you can, tell them in person first, then send the email the same day. Learning about your own job change from an email to all staff is the thing most likely to make this go badly.
- **The paragraph about the phone team's 30% turnover goes beyond what you told me.** You didn't say why people left. If understaffing wasn't a main cause, cut the sentence that says too few people made the work hard. The safety-net sentence can carry that paragraph on its own.
- **"I'll share those answers as soon as we have them" is a promise.** Cut it if you can't keep it.
- **Add your name above "Chief Operating Officer."**
- **I left out anything you didn't know.** That includes evening pay, whether training is paid, what happens to seniority and time off, health coverage, and the other five branches. If you get answers before sending, especially on evening pay or the other branches, add them. Staff will ask about both.
